questions.question: Your key login fails and `ssh -v` shows the key being refused. Which permission problem is the most common cause?
options: The public key file on your laptop is 644
~/.ssh or authorized_keys on the server is writable by group or others
questions.explanation: SSH refuses keys when ~/.ssh or authorized_keys are too open. Required modes are 700 for ~/.ssh and 600 for authorized_keys; 644 for a public key is fine.

questions.question: In `~/.ssh/config` you have a specific `Host web1` block and a `Host *` block. Where should `Host *` go and why?
options: At the end, because SSH uses the first value it finds for each option
At the top, because later blocks override earlier ones
In a separate file, because Host * is not allowed in ~/.ssh/config
questions.explanation: For each option the first obtained value wins, so put specific hosts first and general defaults last. ssh -G host shows the final settings.

questions.question: Which command lets you connect to a private PostgreSQL server at 10.0.1.20:5432 from your laptop on local port 5433, through web1?
questions.explanation: -L opens a listening port on your side (5433) and forwards traffic through web1 to 10.0.1.20:5432. -R opens the port on the server side instead.

questions.question: Why is `ProxyJump` generally preferred over agent forwarding (`ssh -A`) for reaching servers behind a bastion?
options: ProxyJump is faster because it disables encryption on the bastion
With agent forwarding, anyone with root on the remote host can use your agent while you are connected
Agent forwarding only works with RSA keys
ProxyJump copies your private key to the bastion so it can authenticate for you
questions.explanation: ProxyJump keeps the end-to-end connection encrypted from your laptop; the bastion only relays bytes and never gets access to your keys or agent.
